# {{lb|vi|neologism|uncommon}} [[Vietnamese]] "[[traditional]] [[clothing]]s"

====Usage notes====
This is a neologism coined recently to refer to "Vietnamese traditional clothings", modelled after terms from other Sinosphere languages like {{ncog|zh|漢服}}, {{ncog|ko|한복(韓服)}}, {{ncog|ja|和服|tr=wafuku}}. Historically, it was never in use in actual Vietnamese texts prior to, during, and for some time after, the colonial period.

Its usage is still limited to mostly Sinologist circles.

During the colonial period, Vietnamese clothings were simply expressed with phrases like "{{l|vi|[[cách]] [[phục sức]]/[[ăn mặc]] [[của]] [[ta]]||our style of dressing}}" (''Việt Nam phong tục'', 1915), "{{l|vi|[[quần áo]] [[ta]]||our clothings}}" (''Cành hoa điểm tuyết'', 1921), "{{l|vi|[[đồ]] [[An Nam]]||Annamese clothes}}" (''Chúa tàu Kim Quy'', 1923). Slightly later, the term {{m|vi|quốc phục}} started to be used to refer to traditional clothings (''Số đỏ'', 1938; ''Đoạn tình'', 1940).

{{m|vi|đồ ta}} (attested in [http://baochi.nlv.gov.vn/baochi/cgi-bin/baochi?a=d&d=WJMY19350830.2.15&e=-------vi-20--1--img-txIN------ an article in 1935, pg. 3], ''quốc phục'' is also attested here) is the modern term in ''actual'' colloquial usage for Vietnamese-styled clothings.

chuẩn đô đốc.raw:
===Etymology===
{{vi-etym-sino|准|quasi-|都督|admiral}}. In Chinese, Japanese and Korean, {{m|zh|准}}, meaning "quasi-" or "almost", is typically reserved for {{m|zh|准將||brigadier (general); (air) commodore|lit=quasi-general officer}} and {{m|zh|准尉||warrant officer|lit=quasi-junior officer}}, which is an additional fourth or fifth rank just below {{m|zh|少將||major general; rear admiral; air mashal}} or {{m|zh|少尉||first lieutenant; lieutenant junior grade; flying officer}}. {{m|zh|准}} is thus outside the typical prefix scheme which includes {{m|zh|大|pos=highest}}, {{m|zh|上|pos=(second) highest}}, {{m|zh|中|pos=middle}} and {{m|zh|少|pos=lowest}}. For the rank of "rear admiral", the prefix {{m|zh|少}} would be more suitable (compare the army and air counterpart, {{m|vi|thiếu tướng||major general; air vice-marshal}}), but given Vietnamese's comparatively unorthodox and peculiar terminology, it is not used for this naval rank.

===Pronunciation===
{{vi-IPA}}

===Noun===
{{vi-noun|head=[[chuẩn]] [[đô đốc]]}}

# {{lb|vi|military rank|of a navy or coast guard}} a [[rear admiral]]

====Usage notes====
Vietnamese uses three specific terms for the three naval general officer ranks, namely {{m|vi|đô đốc||admiral}}, {{m|vi|phó đô đốc||vice admiral}} and {{m|vi|chuẩn đô đốc||rear admiral}}. In contrast, Chinese, Japanese and Korean use generic terms applicable in all branches, for example {{ncog|ja|大将|tr=taishō||general; admiral; air chief marshal}}, {{m|ja|中将|tr=chūjō||lieutenant general; vice admiral; air mashal}} and {{m|ja|少将|tr=shōshō||major general; vice admiral; air vice-marshal}}; and lower ranks are generically termed, for example {{m|vi|đại tá||colonel; senior colonel; captain; commodore}}.

===See also===
* {{l|vi|đề đốc}}

|text= Những đóng góp to lớn của ông trong cuộc chiến chống '''chủ nghĩa phân biệt chủng tộc''' Apartheid, chống đói nghèo, bất bình đẳng đã được đất nước Nam Phi cùng nhiều quốc gia và các tổ chức quốc tế trên thế giới vinh danh bằng rất nhiều giải thưởng, tiêu biểu là giải thưởng Nobel hòa bình năm 1993, Giải thưởng Lenin của Liên Xô và Giải thưởng Tự do của Mỹ. Ruism professes the rule of people.
Mohism professes the rule of heaven.
Daoism professes the '''rule of none''' / '''anarchism'''.
Legalism professes the rule of law.}} #* {{quote-web|vi|origlang= en|year= 2021|origyear= 1999|work= meomun.noblogs.org|by= Chuck Morse|quotee= Sam Mbah|title= Chủ nghĩa Vô trị châu Phi: phỏng vấn Sam Mbah|titleurl= https://meomun.noblogs.org/post/2021/11/23/chu-nghia-vo-tri-chau-phi-phong-van-sam-mbah/|original= African Anarchism: An Interview with Sam Mbah |text= Mặc dù '''chủ nghĩa vô trị''' không thể hoàn thiện nếu không có sự đóng góp từ Tây Âu, chúng tôi tin rằng nhiều yếu tố của các xã hội châu Phi truyền thống có khả năng góp phần xây dựng các ý tưởng vô trị.
Một trong số đó là truyền thống tự lực, tương trợ hoặc hợp tác rất phổ biến trong xã hội châu Phi. Xã hội này được cấu trúc để giảm thiểu chủ nghĩa cá nhân, còn cách tiếp cận tập thể thì luôn được vận dụng nhằm giải quyết các vấn đề trong đời sống: ở bản chất của nó, tôi nghĩ đó chính là những gì '''chủ nghĩa vô trị''' muốn truyền bá. |origtext= en:Although '''anarchism''' is not complete without the Western European contributions, we believe there are elements of African traditional societies that can be of assistance in elaborating anarchist ideas.
One of these is the self-help, mutual aid, or cooperative tradition that is prevalent in African society. This society is structured such that there is reduced individualism and a collective approach toward solving problems and living life: reduced to its essence, I think that is what '''anarchism''' is preaching.}}

diêu bông.raw:
===Etymology=== As explained by poet {{w|Hoàng Cầm (poet)|Hoàng Cầm}}, who coined the name of the fictional plant, to a friend: "diêu bông" is based on "hoa phiêu diêu" ("the fleeting flower").Vũ Tuấn (23 October 2019) [https://tuoitre.vn/su-that-sau-nhung-tac-pham-de-doi-ky-cuoi-la-dieu-bong-va-vi-dang-tinh-yeu-20191023110538495.htm "Sự thật sau những tác phẩm để đời - Kỳ cuối: Lá diêu bông và vị đắng tình yêu" (The truth behind life's works - Last issue: diêu bông leaf and the bitterness of love)]. ''{{w|Tuổi Trẻ}}'' (in Vietnamese) {{blend|vi|phiêu diêu|t1=floating, fleeting|bông|t2=flower ''(dialectal)''}}. The real-life plant behind the imaginary ''diêu bông'' plant has been identified as {{taxlink|Clerodendrum cyrtophyllum|species}}, known as {{l|vi|bọ mẩy}} or {{l|vi|đắng cẩy}} in Vietnamese. ===Pronunciation=== {{vi-IPA}} ===Noun=== {{vi-noun}} # An imaginary plant, whose leaves an unwed maiden challenges her suitors to find for her in order to marry her #* {{quote-text|vi|year=1959|author=Hoàng Cầm|title=Lá Diêu Bông|lines=5–9 |passage=Chị bảo:
Đứa nào tìm được Lá '''Diêu Bông'''
Từ nay ta gọi là chồng.
Hai ngày em tìm thấy lá
Chị chau mày: Đâu phải Lá '''Diêu Bông'''. |translation=Big Sis said:
Whoever can find the '''Diêu Bông''' Leaf
From now on I will call him my husband.
Two days later, I found the leaf
Big Sis knit her brows[, saying]: Not '''Diêu Bông''' Leaf.}} #* {{quote-text|vi|year=1990|author=Trần Tiến|title=Lá Diêu Bông |passage=Em đố ai tìm được lá '''diêu bông'''
Em xin lấy làm chồng |translation=You challenged thus: whoever could find '''diêu bông''' leaf
You'd fain marry him as your husband}} ===References=== {{reflist}} ===Further reading=== Hoàng Cầm (17 September 2004) [https://nlsbaoloc.info/index.php/su-tim/cau-chuyn-vn-hc-ngh-thut/1427-s-tich-bai-th-la-dieu-bong-hoang-cm "Sự Tích Bài Thơ Lá Diêu Bông" (The Tale of the Poem on Diêu Bông Leaf)] (in Vietnamese)

dính.raw:
===Etymology===
Cognate with {{cog|scb|-}} [Mày] ''patĭŋ³'' (Babaev & Samarina, 2018).

Formally, this looks like a causative prefixed (Proto-Vietic prefix {{m|mkh-vie-pro|*pr-|*pr- ~ *p-}}) derivative of a root. This root is probably of Sinitic origin and related to the modern Sino-Vietnamese morpheme {{vi-link|định||定}}, i.e. "to make fixed" or "to cause to be fixed". Another possibility is that the root is related to {{vi-link|đính||釘}} instead.

|translation=His poetry's musicality is as natural as breaths, as a flowing river, as a gust of afternoon wind next to the veranda, and as pristine as '''nightingales'''’ songs, a symbol of pure poetry, always watching over and waking up his conspecifics from lulling.}}

====Usage notes====
English {{m|en|nightingale}} corresponds to Vietnamese '''dạ oanh''', while {{m|en|hwamei}} corresponds to {{m|vi|họa mi}} (both borrowed from Chinese {{zh-l|*畫眉|painted eye-brow}}. Still, English {{m|en|nightingale}} (and its cognates like Danish {{m|da|nattergal}}) are indeed mistranslated as {{m|vi|họa mi}} (for example, by Nguyễn & Vũ, 1986).<ref>{{w|Hans Christian Andersen|Andersen, Hans Christian}} (author) (1843). "Nattergalen". (1986) [https://thegioicotich.vn/chim-hoa-mi/ Vietnamese translation] by Nguyễn Văn Hải & Vũ Minh Toàn.</ref> As a result, some bilingual Vietnamese-English dictionaries accept the Vietnamese translation {{m|vi|họa mi}} for {{m|en|nightingale}}.<ref>Phan, Văn Giường (2014) ''Tuttle Concise Vietnamese Dictionary: Vietnamese-English English-Vietnamese''. p. 138</ref><ref>''Cambridge English-Vietnamese dictionary''. dầu.raw:
===Pronunciation===
{{vi-IPA}}

===Etymology 1===
{{wp|vi:}}
Unclear.

This is usually considered to be a loan from {{ltc-l|油|id=1}}. There are two points supporting this stance: one, the word was spelled with {{m|vi|油}} in Nôm texts and dictionaries (although this point is not absolute due to the word's unfortunate absence in important texts such as ''Phật thuyết đại báo phụ mẫu ân trọng kinh'' (佛說大報父母恩重經) and ''Quốc âm thi tập'' (國音詩集)),<!-- Cư trần lạc đạo phú, if indeed authored by Trần Nhân Tông, certainly was rewritten in its entirety at a later date using an updated orthography, since its orthography, at least the version on Vietnamese Wikisource, is much more in-line with later Nôm texts, as opposed with the more archaic orthographies of the mentioned texts.--> two, in ''Dictionarium Annamiticum Lusitanum et Latinum'' (1651), a dictionary based chiefly on the Northern dialects and an important document on the then-disappearing contrast between ‹dĕ-› (< Proto-Vietic ''*-t/d-'') and ‹d-› (< PV ''*j-'') in these dialects, only {{m|mkh-mvi|dầu}} is attested, while ''*dĕầu'' is not.<!-- If a word is attested with ‹dĕ-›, it can be said for sure to have earlier *-t/d-, if there is only spelling with ‹d-›, it can generally be considered to have earlier *j-; a very important exception is dâu "mulberry", which certainly came from earlier *-t/d-, but had no spelling with ‹dĕ-› (an instance of dĕâu in Phép giảng tám ngày is a misspelling of dĕấu "mark").-->

On the other hand, as Jacques (2022)<ref>Jacques, Guillaume (2022), "A propos du vietnamien dầu “huile”," Panchronica, 10/08/2022, https://panchr.hypotheses.org/3628 (ISSN 2494-775X)</ref> argued, there are indeed forms such as Kha Phong ''ntuː¹'' and {{cog|thm|-}} ''atuː¹'', for which Ferlus (2007) reconstructed {{cog|mkh-vie-pro|*-tuː||oil}}. Furthermore, there was a word spelled ‹taw›, with the English equivalent ‹Oil› and Chinese equivalent {{m|zh|油|yeo}}, attested in {{w|Sir John Barrow, 1st Baronet|Barrow}} (1806)'s [https://archive.org/details/voyagetocochinch00barr/ A voyage to Cochinchina, in the years 1792 and 1793], recorded either a very aberrant Vietnamese dialect or a Vietnamese-based pidgin of Turon (modern day {{m|vi|Đà Nẵng}}). The name of {{m|vi|thầu dầu||castor oil plant}} (from etymology 2 below) is also likely related, and it has the {{cog|tou|-}} [Cuối Chăm] cognate ''tʌw² tʌw²''.

|text= Ông chủ trương thuyết “'''kiêm ái'''” vì ông cho là giai cấp thống trị, do áp bức bóc lột dân, xa xỉ, lãng phí nên tàn ác. “'''Kiêm ái'''” có nghĩa là yêu thương lẫn nhau, yêu người như yêu mình, xem nhà người như nhà mình, xem nước người như nước mình.
|translation=He promoted the doctrine of “'''inclusive / universal love'''” because he thought that the oppressor class were vicious and cruel because of their extravagance, wastefulness, subjugation and exploitation of the people. “'''Inclusive / universal love'''” means loving each other, loving others as one loves oneself, seeing and treating others' households like one's own household, and seeing and treating other countries like one's own country.}}

ma ăn cỗ.raw:
===Etymology===
From {{af|vi|ma<t:ghost>|ăn<t:eat>|cỗ<t:feast>}}. This refers to the tradition of preparing a feast for the deceased during deathday commemorations or similar events for their ghosts to consume. However, even after the ghosts have allegedly had their meal, the feast remains untouched. It is unknown how or where the ghosts have had their meal, making it a secret.<ref>https://www.sachhayonline.com/tua-sach/giai-thich-thanh-ngu-tuc-ngu/ma-an-co/1784</ref>

===Adjective===

#*:: In the autumn of 1940, when the Japanese '''Fascists''' violated Indochina’s territory to establish new bases in their fight against the Allies, the French imperialists went down on their bended knees and handed over our country to them.
#*: Một dân-tộc đã gan-góc chống ách nô-lệ của Pháp hơn 80 năm nay, một dân-tộc đã gan-góc đứng về phe Đồng minh chống '''Phát-xít''' mấy năm nay, dân-tộc đó phải được tự do! Dân-tộc đó phải được độc lập!

#*: Tống Giang nghe nói níu lấy hai người công sai mà kêu rằng: "Khổ lắm [[trời ơi]]! Thực là '''phúc bất trùng lai, họa vô đơn chí'''!"
#*:: {{w|Song Jiang}}, upon hearing that, clutched the two guards tightly and moaned: "[[good heavens|Good Heavens]], woe is me! Indeed, '''blessings never come in pair; disasters never come singly'''!"
#* '''2011''', Hoàng Đình Trung MD, [https://suckhoedoisong.vn/bao-skds-an-nhan-cua-toi-16943694.htm "Báo SK&ĐS - Ân nhân của tôi (Health and Life Newspaper - My Benefactor)"] ''Health and Life Newspaper''
#*: Chúng tôi [[khẩn trương]] quyết cứu [[sản phụ]] nhưng tình hình mỗi lúc một nguy kịch. Thật là “'''Phúc bất trùng lai, họa vô đơn chí'''”.
#*:: We urgently determined to save the life of the woman in childbirth yet with every moment the situation became more and more critical. Indeed, “'''blessings never come in pair; disasters never come singly'''”.

rượu.raw:
===Etymology===
From {{inh|vi|mkh-vie-pro|*raːwʔ}}. Cognate with {{cog|mtq|-}} Bi {{m|mtq|rão}}, {{cog|tou|-}} [Cuối Chăm] ''riɛw⁴'', Proto-Pong ''*riɛw⁴''. This word is only attested in the more innovative subgroups (Viet-Muong, Tho, Pong), while the more conservative subgroups such as Chutic inheriting reflexes of {{m|mkh-vie-pro|*p-ɗoː}} (originally "yeast", cf. {{ncog|kjg|-}} [Cuang] ''pdoʔ'' ("yeast")) or some other words.

Considering the paucity of cognates, the lack of indication of semantic shift from earlier meaning and that it is a cultural item, this is probably ultimately a loanword, although the origin is not yet clear. However, compare {{cog|tai-pro|*ʰlawꟲ}} (whence {{cog|th|เหล้า}}), as well as these Sino-Tibetan words: {{cog|zh|-}} {{och-l|醪|tr={{IPAfont|*ruːw}}|alcohol with dregs}} (ZS),{{cog|bo|རུ་མ||curdled milk}}, and {{cog|kac|ru||liquor}}.<ref>Schuessler, A. (2007). ''An Etymological Dictionary of Old Chinese''. p. 345</ref>

This is not a cognate nor descendant of {{ncog|zh|-}} {{och-l|酒|tr={{IPAfont|*tsuʔ}}}} (B-S). As indicated by reflexes in other Vietic languages, Vietnamese ‹r-› is inherited and is not the result of spirantization.

thuốc đắng đã tật, sự thật mất lòng.raw:
===Etymology===
{{calque|vi|zh|良藥苦口利於病，忠言逆耳利於行|tr=lương dược khổ khẩu lợi ư bệnh, trung ngôn nghịch nhĩ lợi ư hành}}; ultimately based on a line from ''{{w|Han Feizi}}''.<ref>{{w|Han Fei}} (author); Liao, W. K. (translator) (1959). ''The Complete Works of Han Fei Tzu - Vol. II'', [http://www2.iath.virginia.edu/exist/cocoon/xwomen/texts/hanfei/d2.32/1/0/bilingual "Chapter XXXII. Outer Congeries of Sayings, The Upper Left Series"]. London: A. Probsthain. p. 35. Chinese original:「夫良藥苦於口，而智者勸而飲之，知其入而已己疾也。忠言拂於耳，而明主聽之，知其可以致功也。」; translation: "Indeed, good drugs are bitter to the mouth, but intelligent people are willing to take them because they know the drugs after being taken will cure their diseases. Loyal words are unpleasant to the ears, but the enlightened sovereign listens to them, because he knows they will bring about successful results."</ref>

{{vi-IPA}}

===Phrase===
{{vi-phrase|head=[[thuốc]] [[đắng]] [[đã]] [[tật]], [[sự thật]] [[mất]] [[lòng]]}}

# [[effective]] [[medicine]]s tend to be [[bitter]], and the [[truth]] tends to [[hurt]]

====Usage notes====
* Usually used to say "the truth hurts", but the first half can also be used to convince others to take unpalatable medicines.
* Although this phrase is the etymological form, it's more commonly seen in variants such as {{m|vi|thuốc đắng dã tật, sự thật mất lòng}} or {{m|vi|thuốc đắng giã tật, sự thật mất lòng}}.

tiếng.raw:
===Etymology===
Ultimately from {{der|vi|zh|-}} {{ltc-l|聲}}, likely through a {{bor|vi|tai}} language (compare {{cog|th|เสียง}}) since the tonal correspondence is atypical for a direct borrowing. Cognate with {{cog|mtq|thiểng}}, {{cog|nuo|thiếng}}.

Attested as {{m|mkh-mvi|tiếng}} in the ''Dictionarium Annamiticum Lusitanum et Latinum'' (1651).

===Pronunciation===
{{vi-IPA}}
* {{homophone|vi|tiến|Tiến}}

===Noun===
{{vi-noun|[[㗂]], [[𪱐]]|cls={{vi-l|cái}}, {{vi-l|thứ}}|sort=tieng}}

# [[voice]]
#: {{uxi|vi|tắt '''tiếng'''|to lose one's voice}}
# [[sound]]
#: {{uxi|vi|'''tiếng''' súng|(sound of a) gunshot}}
#: {{uxi|vi|'''tiếng''' sủa|bark (of a dog)}}
# [[language]]
#: {{uxi|vi|nói ba thứ '''tiếng'''|to speak three languages}}
# [[reputation]] or [[renown]]
#: {{uxi|vi|nổi tiếng|famous}}
#: {{uxi|vi|khét tiếng|infamous; notorious}}
#: {{uxi|vi|danh tiếng / tiếng tăm|reputation}}
#: {{uxi|vi|tiếng thơm|fame for being a paragon|lit=fragrant fame}}
#: {{ux|vi|Tiếng thơm còn mãi cho muôn đời sau.|They will forever be known by later generations as the paragon of virtue.}}
# {{lb|vi|linguistics}} [[syllable]]
# {{lb|vi|linguistics|colloquial}} [[dialect]]
# {{lb|vi|linguistics|prosody|colloquial}} [[accent]]
#: {{ux|vi|[[thằng cha|Thằng cha]] đó nói '''tiếng''' Quảng Ngãi tao không nghe được.|He speaks the Quãng Ngãi accent and I can't make sense of it.}}
# {{lb|vi|colloquial}} [[hour]]
#: {{ux|vi|Nó ngồi đọc truyện suốt năm '''tiếng'''.|He's been sitting there reading manga for five hours.}}

====Usage notes====
* ''tiếng'' meaning "language" is often used in compound words (eg. ''[[tiếng Anh]]'' "[[English]]") rather than as a [[free morpheme]], similar to the Chinese {{m|zh|文}} ([[Sino-Vietnamese|SV]]: ''{{m|vi|văn}}'') and {{m|ja|語}} (SV: ''[[ngữ]]''). The latter two are sometimes used in a Sino-Vietnamese manner (eg. ''[[Pháp văn]]'' "[[French]]", ''[[Hoa ngữ]]'' "[[Chinese]]"). If one wishes to refer to "language" as a [[standalone]] term in formal contexts, ''[[ngôn ngữ]]'' is used instead. In informal contexts, one may use for instance ''ba thứ tiếng'' to mean "three languages".
* The word ''[[âm]]'' is used instead of ''tiếng'' to mean a sound made by a [[television]] set, a [[radio]], or another device that imitates or reproduces the sounds of other objects. ''Âm'' is also used in phonetics.
* ''tiếng'' meaning "hour" is used in casual speech to refer to a '''period of time''', to avoid confusion with ''giờ''. ''giờ'' is used to refer to either a period of time or a '''point in time''' in formal context (for example, ''năm giờ'' means either "five hours" or "five o'clock"). One may also use ''tiếng {{l|vi|đồng hồ}}'' or ''giờ đồng hồ'' to refer to a period of time.

====Synonyms====
* {{sense|sound}} {{l|vi|âm}} (see [[#Usage note|usage note]] above)
* {{sense|language}} {{l|vi|ngôn ngữ}}; {{l|vi|ngữ}}
* {{sense|syllable}} {{l|vi|âm tiết}}; {{l|vi|vần}}
* {{sense|dialect}} {{l|vi|phương ngữ}}; {{l|vi|phương ngôn}}
* {{sense|accent}} {{l|vi|giọng}}; {{l|vi|khẩu âm}}
* {{sense|hour}} {{l|vi|giờ}}

trầu quơ.raw:
===Alternative forms===
* {{alt|vi|trầu quâu}} (''Nẫu'' dialects with more complete {{IPAfont|/əːj/ - /oj/}} merger)

===Etymology===
See {{m|vi|trời ơi}}. This phrase shows several sound changes in the {{m|vi|Nẫu}} dialects: the incomplete {{IPAfont|/əːj/ - /oj/}} merger, the subsequent {{IPAfont|/oj > əw/}} shift, and finally the {{IPAfont|/əːj > əːˠ/}} shift of the rest of items with {{IPAfont|/əːj/}}. The {{IPAfont|/w/}} in ''quơ'' seems to be sporadic linking {{IPAfont|/w/}}.
* {{IPAfont|/ʈəːj<sup>A2</sup> əːj<sup>A1</sup>/ > /ʈoj<sup>A2</sup> əːj<sup>A1</sup>/}} (incomplete {{IPAfont|/əːj/ - /oj/}} merger) > {{IPAfont|/ʈəw<sup>A2</sup> əːj<sup>A1</sup>/}} ({{IPAfont|/oj > əw/}} shift) > {{IPAfont|/ʈəw<sup>A2</sup> əːˠ<sup>A1</sup>/}} ({{IPAfont|/əːj > əːˠ/}} shift of the rest of {{IPAfont|/əːj/}}) > {{IPAfont|/ʈəw<sup>A2</sup> wəːˠ<sup>A1</sup>/}} (sporadic linking {{IPAfont|/w/}}).

This form seems to be more common in {{w|Bình Định}}, while {{m|vi|trầu quâu}} is more common in {{w|Phú Yên}}, where {{IPAfont|/əːj/ - /oj/}} merger was more completed. Although it seems that there is no ''Nẫu'' dialect where the merger was fully completed.

tùng cúc trúc mai.raw:
===Alternative forms===
* {{l|vi|tùng trúc cúc mai}}

===Etymology===
{{vi-etym-sino|松|pine|菊|chrysanthemum|竹|bamboo|梅|plum, apricot}}, said to represent "winter", "autumn", "summer", "spring" respectively.

Compare the concepts of {{w|Flowers of the Four Seasons}} and {{w|Four Gentlemen}}.

Certain sources explain the reverse order of the seasons as due to European influence, where paintings (and writings, etc.) are views from left-to-right, as opposed to the traditional order in the Sinosphere, being right-to-left. However, this is far-fetched as {{m|vi|tùng cúc||pine and chrysanthemum}} and {{m|vi|trúc mai||bamboo and apricot}} are both common motifs in Vietnamese literature long before European influence, signifying a person's spirit, and intimate bonds, respectively (and both also seems to be borrowed from/influenced by Chinese literature).

Most likely this phrase was just amalgamation of those two compounds above, then forcefully made to fit with similar concepts to which it shares several elements (see {{m|zh|松竹梅|tr=tùng trúc mai}}), even if the order of seasons is reverse.

===Pronunciation===
{{vi-IPA}}

===Noun===

tạnh.raw:

Unclear. 

Usages suggest possible conflation of two different etyma {{bor+|vi|ltc|-|nocap=y}}. Namely:
* {{ltc-l|靜|to be still}} (SV: {{m|vi|tĩnh}}) or {{ltc-l|靖|‘to be still’ → ‘to still’}} (SV: {{m|vi|tĩnh}}); if true, then the tonal, register, and rhyme correspondences are still typical for an early loan, and

vác.raw:
===Etymology===
Probably a loanword from a neighboring {{bor|vi|aav}} language, potentially even from a {{bor|vi|mkh-vie}} language.
Compare Toum ''baːk⁷'' ("to carry on shoulder"), {{cog|puo|-}} ''beːk'', {{cog|kha|bah||to carry on one's back, to bear}}, {{cog|pac|báq||to carry slung under one shoulder}}, {{cog|kns|-}} ''baʔ'' ("to carry child in a cloth on one's back"), {{cog|oyb|-}} ''baʔ'' ("to carry on back"). Khasian, Bahnaric, Katuic and other Vietic languages all point to the implosive ''*ɓ-'', from which the Vietnamese form ''cannot'' be derived from through regular sound changes (the expected form would be ''*mác'' instead). <!-- Aslian and Khmuic neutralized PAA *ɓ and *b into *b. -->

Compare also {{cog|kac|bà'||carry a child on the back}}, {{cog|zh|-}} {{och-l|負|tr={{IPAfont|*[b]əʔ}}}} (B-S), {{cog|raw|baq||to carry on back or shoulder}}. <!-- While these two sets are most likely related one way or another, the donor of Vietnamese certainly is not a Trans-Himalayan language, as the Sinitic form had *-ʔ while the Ngwi/Loloish forms are open syllable, neither of which can give Vietnamese -k. -->

đánh vần.raw:
===Pronunciation===
{{vi-IPA}}

===Verb===
{{vi-verb}}

# {{lb|vi|linguistics}} to [[spell]] a [[Vietnamese]] [[syllable]] as you [[pronounce]] it
#: ''Cách '''đánh vần''' từ "toán": o a nờ oan, tờ oan toan sắc toán''

====Usage notes====
* This word is frequently simplistically used to translate the English verb ''to'' {{m|en|spell}}, although ''to spell'' a word does not mean to pronounce it.
* To ''đánh vần'' a syllable, first you spell the '''[[rhyme]]''' (and also any letter that represents the [[glide]] [[phoneme]] /w/, except as in ''qu'' /kw/, if any); then you pronounce the rhyme:
** As in the above example of the word ''toán'', you list three letters: "o" (letter ''o'') for the glide /w/, "a" (letter "a") and "nờ" (letter ''n'') for the rhyme; then you pronounce "oan".
* Secondly, you add the '''initial [[consonant]] letter''', pronounce the outcome syllable, then add the '''[[tone]]''', then pronounce the final outcome.
** After you have "oan", you say "tờ" (letter ''t''), then say "toan", then say "sắc" (''sắc'' tone), then finish by saying "toán'.
* To sum up, this is what you say to ''đánh vần'' the word ''toán'': "o (letter ''o'') a (letter ''a'') nờ (letter ''n'') oan, tờ (letter ''t'') oan toan sắc (''sắc'' tone) toán".

đểu cáng.raw:
===Etymology===
{{com|vi|đểu|cáng}}.

Element {{m|vi|đểu}} originally meant possibly "burden ~ load"<ref name = "daf-deu">{{cite-book|author= J.F.M. Génibrel|year= 1898|title= Dictionnaire Annamite-Français|entry= Đểu|page= 211|pageurl= https://chunom.org/pages/genibrel/#211}}</ref> then "person who carries burdens ~ loads, porter"<ref name = "daf-deu"/> or specifically "hired porter using a shoulder pole",<ref name = "vth">{{cite-web|vi|author= Vương Trung Hiếu|year= 2021|url= https://thanhnien.vn/lat-leo-chu-nghia-deu-cang-va-cuu-van-post1403367.html|title=Lắt léo chữ nghĩa: ‘Đểu cáng’ và ‘cửu vạn’|trans-title= Conundrum about Words and Meanings: ‘Đểu cáng’ and ‘cửu vạn’|work= {{w|Thanh Niên}}|trans-work= Young People}}</ref> while element {{m|vi|cáng}} originally meant "hammock on a carrying pole",<ref name = "daf-cang">{{cite-book|author= J.F.M. Génibrel|year= 1898|title= Dictionnaire Annamite-Français|entry= Cáng|page= 64|pageurl= https://chunom.org/pages/genibrel/#64}}</ref><ref name = "tgk-cang">{{cite-book|year= 2004|author= Rev. An-tôn Trần Gia Kiệm|title= Giúp đọc Nôm và Hán-Việt|entry= Cáng|page= 290|pageurl= https://archive.org/details/giupdocnomvahanviet/page/290/mode/2up}}</ref><ref name = vth/> then "hammock-carrier".<ref name = "vth"/> All those taken together, this compound word was originally a collective noun meaning formerly "porters, carriers" yet nowadays "the nobodies, the bad lot".<ref name = "tgk-deu">{{cite-book|year= 2004|author= Rev. An-tôn Trần Gia Kiệm|title= Giúp đọc Nôm và Hán-Việt|entry= Đểu|page= 386|pageurl= https://archive.org/details/giupdocnomvahanviet/page/386/mode/2up}}</ref><ref name = "tgk-cang"/>

{{w|Vương Trung Hiếu}} (2021) presents an unsourced viewpoint that both {{m|vi|đểu}} and '''đểu cáng''' nowadays mean "cads, scoundrels, rascals (n.)" → "caddish (adj.)" because poorly-educated porters often dealt unfairly with one another and competed against each other for customers by means of cheating and violence.<ref name = "vth">{{cite-web|vi|author= Vương Trung Hiếu|year= 2021|url= https://thanhnien.vn/lat-leo-chu-nghia-deu-cang-va-cuu-van-post1403367.html|title=Lắt léo chữ nghĩa: ‘Đểu cáng’ và ‘cửu vạn’|trans-title= Conundrum about Words and Meanings: ‘Đểu cáng’ and ‘cửu vạn’|work= {{w|Thanh Niên}}|trans-work= Young People}}</ref>
